# go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-Constrained  Hyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices

units.text: ###### Abstract
context: go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-Constrained  Hyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices

units.text: Doubly stochastic matrices enable learned mixing across residual streams, but parameterizing the set of doubly stochastic matrices (the Birkhoff polytope) exactly and efficiently remains an open challenge. Existing exact methods scale factorially with the number of streams (<!-- MathML: <math alttext="d" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="abstract1.m1" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> --> dd), while Kronecker-factorized approaches are efficient but expressivity-limited. We introduce a novel exact parameterization grounded in the theory of generalized orthostochastic matrices, which scales as <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathcal{O}(d^{3})" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="abstract1.m2" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(d^{3})</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝒪⁡(d3)\mathcal{O}(d^{3}) and exposes a single hyperparameter <!-- MathML: <math alttext="s" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="abstract1.m3" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> --> ss which continuously interpolates between a computationally efficient boundary and the fully expressive Birkhoff polytope. Building on Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC), a framework for learned dynamic layer connectivity, we instantiate this parameterization in go-mHC. Our method composes naturally with Kronecker-factorized methods, substantially recovering expressivity at similar FLOP costs. Spectral analysis indicates that go-mHC fills the Birkhoff polytope far more completely than Kronecker-factorized baselines. On synthetic stream-mixing tasks, go-mHC achieves the minimum theoretical loss while converging up to <!-- MathML: <math alttext="10\times" class="ltx_math_unparsed" display="inline" id="abstract1.m4" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\times</annotation></semantics></math> --> 10×10\times faster. We validate our approach in a 30M parameter GPT-style language model. The expressivity, efficiency, and exactness of go-mHC offer a practical avenue for scaling <!-- MathML: <math alttext="d" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="abstract1.m5" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> --> dd as a new dimension of model capacity.

units.text: ## 1 Introduction
context: go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-Constrained  Hyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices

units.text:
The performance and stability of modern machine learning models increasingly depends on the geometric structure of their underlying matrix parameterizations ([Bronstein et al., 2021](#bib.bib33 ""); [Arjovsky et al., 2016](#bib.bib34 ""); [Saxe et al., 2014](#bib.bib35 ""); [Zhao et al., 2025](#bib.bib38 "")). While traditional constraints—such as symmetry or orthogonality—have long served as foundational tools ([Arjovsky et al., 2016](#bib.bib34 ""); [Wisdom et al., 2016](#bib.bib36 ""); [Henaff et al., 2017](#bib.bib37 "")), recent breakthroughs have pivoted toward more complex geometric structures ([Papillon et al., 2025](#bib.bib32 ""); [Bronstein et al., 2021](#bib.bib33 "")).
A promising frontier for addressing these limitations lies in leveraging manifold theory to map unconstrained optimization spaces onto computationally tractable, constrained geometries ([Xie et al., 2026](#bib.bib1 ""); [Chen et al., 2026](#bib.bib40 ""); [Smith, 2014](#bib.bib39 ""); [Lu et al., 2021](#bib.bib41 "")). Of particular interest is the Birkhoff polytope ([Adams and Zemel, 2011](#bib.bib31 ""); [Tay et al., 2020](#bib.bib26 ""); [Sander et al., 2022](#bib.bib25 ""); [Xie et al., 2026](#bib.bib1 "")), the manifold of doubly stochastic matrices. By enforcing unit row and column sum constraints, the Birkhoff polytope offers a rigorous framework for learning permutations, alignments, and hyper-connections, yet its practical utility has been bottlenecked by the trade-off between exactness and computational scalability ([Xie et al., 2026](#bib.bib1 "")).
context: go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-Constrained  Hyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices

units.text: [Sander et al. (2022)](#bib.bib25 "") demonstrated that constraining the attention pattern to doubly stochastic matrices both improved accuracy in vision and language models while providing an elegant interpretation of learned parameters as probability trajectories ([Sander et al., 2022](#bib.bib25 ""); [Shahbazi et al., 2025](#bib.bib42 "")). [Tay et al. (2020)](#bib.bib26 "") investigated memory-efficient implementations of Sinkhorn Attention due to it’s ability to mix internal representations and have an associated smooth optimization landscape.
context: go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-Constrained  Hyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices

units.text:
A more recent application of such manifold constraints is in the generalization of residual connections ([Sander et al., 2022](#bib.bib25 ""); [Xie et al., 2026](#bib.bib1 "")).
Residual connections have become a crucial component in stabilizing the training of deep neural networks ([He et al., 2015](#bib.bib7 ""); [He et al., 2016](#bib.bib43 "")) and a critical building block of modern large language models ([Radford et al., 2019](#bib.bib21 ""); [Vaswani et al., 2023](#bib.bib20 "")).
Ongoing work investigates dynamic generalizations of the residual streams aimed at increasing the topological complexity of residual function connectivity by increasing the number of streams, <!-- MathML: <math alttext="d" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S1.p3.m1" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> --> dd, while preserving the identity mapping property of the residual stream ([Zhu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib2 "")).

units.text: Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) ([Xie et al., 2026](#bib.bib1 "")) provides evidence that constraining the residual connections to the interior of the Birkhoff polytope significantly improves training stability and scalability. These dynamic generalizations reveal the possibility for a new scaling dimension complementing that of traditional scaling laws: the number of residual streams, <!-- MathML: <math alttext="d" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S1.p4.m1" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> --> dd. Follow-up works have already implemented mHC as the default backbone due to its superior modeling capabilities ([Cheng et al., 2026](#bib.bib44 "")).
context: go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-Constrained  Hyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices

units.text:
In order to further explore the feasibility of this scaling dimension, two works have since introduced the use of exact parameterizations to prevent error accumulation across layers ([Yang and Gao, 2026](#bib.bib3 ""); [Zhou et al., 2026](#bib.bib6 "")). These methods additionally avoid the overhead introduced by iterative normalization and overcome the need for custom infrastructure optimization.mHC-lite ([Yang and Gao, 2026](#bib.bib3 "")) invokes the Birkhoff–von Neumann theorem to parameterize <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathcal{H}^{\text{res}}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S1.p5.m1" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mtext>res</mtext></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}^{\text{res}}</annotation></semantics></math> --> ℋres\mathcal{H}^{\text{res}} as a convex combination of all <!-- MathML: <math alttext="d!" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S1.p5.m2" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>!</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d!</annotation></semantics></math> --> d!d! permutation matrices.
However, the <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathcal{O}(d\cdot d!)" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S1.p5.m3" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>!</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(d\cdot d!)</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝒪⁡(d⋅d!)\mathcal{O}(d\cdot d!) parameter count explodes super-exponentially: at <!-- MathML: <math alttext="d=8" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S1.p5.m4" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d=8</annotation></semantics></math> --> d=8d=8, <!-- MathML: <math alttext="8!=40{,}320" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S1.p5.m5" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>!</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>40,320</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8!=40{,}320</annotation></semantics></math> --> 8!=40,3208!=40{,}320 permutations are required, rendering this approach memory-prohibitive without sampling approximations that restore an approximation gap.
Conversely, KromHC ([Zhou et al., 2026](#bib.bib6 "")) uses the Kronecker products of small doubly stochastic matrices to achieve exact constraints at <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathcal{O}(d^{2})" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S1.p5.m6" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(d^{2})</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝒪⁡(d2)\mathcal{O}(d^{2}) complexity, but in doing so, severely trades off expresivity.

units.text:
We propose a complementary solution rooted in the algebraic theory of generalized orthostochastic matrices ([Gutkin, 2013](#bib.bib45 ""); [Nechita et al., 2023](#bib.bib4 ""); [Korzekwa et al., 2018](#bib.bib47 ""); [Shahbeigi et al., 2021](#bib.bib46 "")).
Our framework for exactly learning doubly stochastic matrices attempts to balance the need for efficiency and expressivity, while exposing a hyperparameter <!-- MathML: <math alttext="s" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S1.p6.m1" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> --> ss that allows for tunability across these attributes. This opens up the possibility for further exploration and new approaches towards scaling Hyper-Connections.
context: go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-Constrained  Hyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices

units.text: In this work, we focus on mHC as an example application, but our generalized orthostochastic construction (go-mHC) can be applied more broadly as a way to parameterize and learn the interior of the Birkhoff polytope. We characterize our parameterization in the context of a synthetic data task mixing <!-- MathML: <math alttext="d" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S1.p7.m1" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> --> dd residual streams and a 30M parameter GPT-style language model.
context: go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-Constrained  Hyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices

units.text: ##### Residual connections and their generalizations.
context: go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-Constrained  Hyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices

units.text:
He et al. ([He et al., 2015](#bib.bib7 "")) introduced skip connections that enable gradient flow via identity shortcuts in ResNets.
This paradigm has evolved to become a key component in the design of large language models (LLMs) owing to its stability and scalability ([Vaswani et al., 2023](#bib.bib20 ""); [Radford et al., 2019](#bib.bib21 "")).
DenseNet ([Huang et al., 2018](#bib.bib12 "")), FractalNet ([Larsson et al., 2017](#bib.bib28 "")), and subsequent works explored richer connectivity patterns passing intermediate features across networks. Other works have explored novel ways of increasing the effective size of the residual stream ([Mak and Flanigan, 2025](#bib.bib29 ""); [Pagliardini et al., 2024](#bib.bib30 ""); [Xie et al., 2023](#bib.bib19 ""); [Baykal et al., 2023](#bib.bib22 "")), examples include: ResiDual ([Xie et al., 2023](#bib.bib19 "")), which explored improvements to layer normalization by doubling the size of the residual stream, and AltUp ([Baykal et al., 2023](#bib.bib22 "")), which widened the effective hidden dimension while maintaining low compute by processing partitioned representations in different layers.
context: go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-Constrained  Hyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices

units.text:
Hyper-Connections (HC) ([Zhu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib2 "")) proposed the first learnable, multi-stream generalization of residual streams allowing for dynamic mixing matrices. A sketch of one such residual block is shown in the green box of figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-ConstrainedHyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices"). HC can theoretically enable models to learn depth and width connections to dynamically rearrange layer connectivity and potentially adds a new avenue for scaling.
Multiple approaches have expanded on this work since, such as splitting
the feature dimension into independent sub-streams ([Zhu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib5 "")) and applying HC to vision and graph neural networks ([Zhu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib2 ""); [Mishra, 2026](#bib.bib23 "")).
context: go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-Constrained  Hyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices

units.text: However, the unconstrained dynamic connectivity of residual blocks in HC removes the explicit guarantee of the identity property – introducing the risk of gradient instability after repeated applications of the mixing terms ([Xie et al., 2026](#bib.bib1 "")). This instability impacts deep networks and restricts scalability due to vanishing and exploding gradients. Subsequent works investigate constraining this connectivity to a manifold that bounds gradient updates through the spectral norm in order to address this instability.
context: go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-Constrained  Hyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices

units.text: ##### Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections.
context: go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-Constrained  Hyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices

units.text: While mHC attempts to enforce this constraint after weight updates using the Sinkhorn-Knopp (SK) algorithm ([Knopp and Sinkhorn, 1967](#bib.bib8 "")), an iterative normalization method for generating doubly stochastic matrices, recent works ([Yang and Gao, 2026](#bib.bib3 ""); [Zhou et al., 2026](#bib.bib6 "")) aim to build HC networks where the learned map is exactly constrained to the polytope. This has two major implications: 1. implementing the SK kernel requires careful kernel-level optimization for efficiency, and 2. finite SK iterations introduce an approximation gap that accumulates with network depth.

units.text: mHC-lite ([Yang and Gao, 2026](#bib.bib3 "")) attempts to circumvent the approximation gap and customized kernel by making use of the Birkhoff–von Neumann theorem to define the learned connections as a convex combination of the <!-- MathML: <math alttext="d!" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.m1" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>!</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d!</annotation></semantics></math> --> d!d! permutation matrices (where <!-- MathML: <math alttext="d" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.m2" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> --> dd is the number of residual streams), at an <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathcal{O}(dC\cdot d!)" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.m3" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>!</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(dC\cdot d!)</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝒪⁡(d​C⋅d!)\mathcal{O}(dC\cdot d!) cost. KromHC ([Zhou et al., 2026](#bib.bib6 "")) sacrifices expressivity and complete coverage of <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathsf{B}_{d}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.m6" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝖡</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathsf{B}_{d}</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝖡d\mathsf{B}_{d} by using tensor products to train residual connections on a much smaller set of exactly double-stochastic matrices with the added benefit of costing only <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathcal{O}(d^{2}C)" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.m7" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(d^{2}C)</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝒪⁡(d2​C)\mathcal{O}(d^{2}C).

units.text: ##### Cayley transforms in neural networks.
context: go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-Constrained  Hyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices

units.text:
The Cayley transform has been used to parameterize orthogonal matrices in recurrent networks ([Helfrich et al., 2018](#bib.bib9 "")), and comparisons with the matrix exponential show similar quality and better stability at lower FLOP cost ([Lezcano-Casado and Martínez-Rubio, 2019](#bib.bib10 "")).
Li et al. ([Li et al. (2020)](#bib.bib11 "")) further demonstrate that iterative Cayley-based optimization outperforms matrix exponential approaches for Stiefel manifold problems.
context: go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-Constrained  Hyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices

units.text: ##### Doubly Stochastic & Orthostochastic matrices.
context: go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-Constrained  Hyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices

units.text:
Multiple works have investigated the use of doubly stochastic matrices in the context of neural network parameterization ([Sander et al., 2022](#bib.bib25 ""); [Adams and Zemel, 2011](#bib.bib31 ""); [Tay et al., 2020](#bib.bib26 "")). [Gutkin (2013)](#bib.bib45 "") introduced generalized orthostochastic matrices, and more recently, [Nechita et al. (2023)](#bib.bib4 "") proved that the set of generalized <!-- MathML: <math alttext="s" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> --> ss-orthostochastic matrices is contained in <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathsf{B}_{d}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝖡</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathsf{B}_{d}</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝖡d\mathsf{B}_{d} and spans all of <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathsf{B}_{d}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝖡</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathsf{B}_{d}</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝖡d\mathsf{B}_{d} as <!-- MathML: <math alttext="s\to\infty" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m4" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s\to\infty</annotation></semantics></math> --> s→∞s\to\infty. Other works have investigated further properties of the spectral span of the Birkhoff polytope ([Kim and Kim, 2022](#bib.bib52 "")) and the geometry of <!-- MathML: <math alttext="s" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m5" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> --> ss-orthostochastic matrices in the quantum setting ([Zyczkowski et al., 2003](#bib.bib15 ""); [Korzekwa et al., 2018](#bib.bib47 ""); [Shahbeigi et al., 2021](#bib.bib46 "")).
These theoretical foundations underlie our choice of parameterization.
To our knowledge, we are the first to apply this construction in a machine learning setting and, more specifically, to learned residual stream routing in deep networks.

This is also advantageous due to the path-connectedness of the special orthogonal group, the group of all “pure” rotations in <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathbb{R}^{d}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S3.SS3.p2.m3" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> --> ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} – more on this in appendix [B.7](#A2.SS7 "B.7 Proofs of Coverage, Path Connectedness and Gradient Stability ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Derivations and Numerical Analysis ‣ go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-ConstrainedHyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices").

units.text: By leveraging the Cayley transform to map learned parameters onto <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathbf{Q}_{l}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S3.SS3.p3.m1" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐐</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{Q}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝐐l\mathbf{Q}_{l}, the necessity for a softmax activation on the inputs is bypassed. The Cayley transform is inherently norm-preserving which ensures numerical stability without the need for the additional normalization step. We suspect that this replacement of softmax with the Cayley transform is one of the reasons that go-mHC accelerates convergence, due to its avoidance of the saturation regions of the exponential function (see results in section [5](#S5 "5 Convergence ‣ go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-ConstrainedHyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices")). While additionally mitigating potential vanishing gradients (appendix [B.10](#A2.SS10 "B.10 Gradient Vanishing and Crosstalk in mHC-lite ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Derivations and Numerical Analysis ‣ go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-ConstrainedHyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices")) and maintaining a well-conditioned Jacobian throughout training. These vanishing gradients trade-off how close mixing matrices near the boundary of the polytope can be learned and the ability to “unlearn them” and return to the Barycenter.

units.text: While KromHC is the most efficient of the proposed methods, it imposes a symmetry on the <!-- MathML: <math alttext="d" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.m1" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> --> dd-streams that significantly prunes the space of potential mixing terms in <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathcal{H}^{\text{res}}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.m2" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mtext>res</mtext></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}^{\text{res}}</annotation></semantics></math> --> ℋres\mathcal{H}^{\text{res}}, as shown in figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1 Spectral Reach of 𝖡_𝑑 Subsets ‣ 4 Expressivity ‣ go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-ConstrainedHyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices")c. We demonstrate that KromHC parameterizes only a sparse subset of <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathsf{B}_{d}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.m3" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝖡</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathsf{B}_{d}</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝖡d\mathsf{B}_{d} for <!-- MathML: <math alttext="d>2" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.m4" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>></mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d>2</annotation></semantics></math> --> d>2d>2 by analyzing the spectral reach of <!-- MathML: <math alttext="k" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.m5" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> --> kk-fold Kronecker products. Specifically, we prove that the spectral space of a <!-- MathML: <math alttext="k" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.m6" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> --> kk-fold Kronecker product of doubly stochastic matrices is invariant to the index <!-- MathML: <math alttext="k" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.m7" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> --> kk, effectively restricting the expressive reach of the resulting constraint to that of its constituent base manifold. A formal proof of this invariance is provided in Appendix [B.3.1](#A2.SS3.SSS1 "B.3.1 Proof of 𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼(𝐀_𝑗)⊆𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼(⨂{𝐀_𝑖}) ‣ B.3 Spectral Equivalence of 𝑘-fold and 1-fold Kronecker Products ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Derivations and Numerical Analysis ‣ go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-ConstrainedHyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices").

units.text: To illustrate this expressivity bottleneck, consider the <!-- MathML: <math alttext="4\times 4" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.m1" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4\times 4</annotation></semantics></math> --> 4×44\times 4 case where <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}\in\mathsf{B}_{2}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.m2" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐀</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐁</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>𝖡</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}\in\mathsf{B}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝐀,𝐁∈𝖡2\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}\in\mathsf{B}_{2}. Their individual spectra are defined as <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\{1,\lambda_{A}\}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.m3" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{1,\lambda_{A}\}</annotation></semantics></math> --> {1,λA}\\{1,\lambda_{A}\\} and <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\{1,\lambda_{B}\}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.m4" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{1,\lambda_{B}\}</annotation></semantics></math> --> {1,λB}\\{1,\lambda_{B}\\} for <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\lambda\in[-1,1]" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.m5" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda\in[-1,1]</annotation></semantics></math> --> λ∈[−1,1]\lambda\in[-1,1]. The spectrum of the Kronecker product <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{B}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.m6" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐀</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><mi>𝐁</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{B}</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝐀⊗𝐁\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{B} is thus <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\{1,\lambda_{A},\lambda_{B},\lambda_{A}\lambda_{B}\}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.m7" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{1,\lambda_{A},\lambda_{B},\lambda_{A}\lambda_{B}\}</annotation></semantics></math> --> {1,λA,λB,λA​λB}\\{1,\lambda_{A},\lambda_{B},\lambda_{A}\lambda_{B}\\}. Crucially, since the product <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\lambda_{A}\lambda_{B}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.m8" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{A}\lambda_{B}</annotation></semantics></math> --> λA​λB\lambda_{A}\lambda_{B} remains real and within the interval <!-- MathML: <math alttext="[-1,1]" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.m9" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[-1,1]</annotation></semantics></math> --> [−1,1][-1,1], the resulting eigenvalues are strictly contained within the spectral hull of <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathsf{B}_{2}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.m10" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝖡</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathsf{B}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝖡2\mathsf{B}_{2} (see Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1 Spectral Reach of 𝖡_𝑑 Subsets ‣ 4 Expressivity ‣ go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-ConstrainedHyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices")b for emperical results and a full proof in [B.3.1](#A2.SS3.SSS1 "B.3.1 Proof of 𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼(𝐀_𝑗)⊆𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼(⨂{𝐀_𝑖}) ‣ B.3 Spectral Equivalence of 𝑘-fold and 1-fold Kronecker Products ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Derivations and Numerical Analysis ‣ go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-ConstrainedHyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices")). Due to this closure, the spectral reach of the Kronecker-parameterized manifold is invariant to the number of products and fails to expand into the broader Karpelevič region available to the full Birkhoff polytope, representing increasingly smaller fractions of the full polytope. By volume, this is a negligible portion of the full <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathsf{B}_{d}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.m11" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝖡</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathsf{B}_{d}</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝖡d\mathsf{B}_{d} when <!-- MathML: <math alttext="d>i_{k}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.m12" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>></mo><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d>i_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> --> d>ikd>i_{k}, and we show emperically in appendix [B.3.2](#A2.SS3.SSS2 "B.3.2 Effect of 𝑑 on approximation error in KromHC ‣ B.3 Spectral Equivalence of 𝑘-fold and 1-fold Kronecker Products ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Derivations and Numerical Analysis ‣ go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-ConstrainedHyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices") that this translates to a <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathcal{O}(d)" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.m13" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(d)</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝒪⁡(d)\mathcal{O}(d) additional error in the minimum achievable loss compared to mHC-lite and go-mHC.

units.text: The collapse in spectral volume for Kronecker-based transforms represents a significant loss in functional diversity. Specifically, these constraints fail to represent cyclic permutations of order greater than <!-- MathML: <math alttext="i_{k}=2" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p3.m1" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i_{k}=2</annotation></semantics></math> --> ik=2i_{k}=2 (e.g., <!-- MathML: <math alttext="1\to 2\to 3\to 1" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p3.m2" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\to 2\to 3\to 1</annotation></semantics></math> --> 1→2→3→11\to 2\to 3\to 1), effectively preventing the model from learning complex periodic dependencies. Furthermore, the restriction to real eigenvalues in the <!-- MathML: <math alttext="2\times 2" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p3.m3" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\times 2</annotation></semantics></math> --> 2×22\times 2 base case implies that the system can only model pure diffusion (information spreading) without advection (directed rotation of information), severely limiting the directional flow of signals within the reservoir.

In unconstrained HC, experiments show negligible incurred FLOP complexity (<!-- MathML: <math alttext="\approx 0.15\%" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom /><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>0.15</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 0.15\%</annotation></semantics></math> --> ≈0.15%\approx 0.15\\% increase) during a forward pass in a 7B parameter model ([Zhu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib2 "")). Projecting onto a manifold with <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathcal{P}_{\mathsf{M}}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS3.p1.m2" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mi>𝖬</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{P}_{\mathsf{M}}</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝒫𝖬\mathcal{P}_{\mathsf{M}} incurs an additional FLOP complexity due to the procedure introduced by <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathsf{M}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS3.p1.m3" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝖬</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathsf{M}</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝖬\mathsf{M}. In mHC, this is significant (<!-- MathML: <math alttext="\approx 8\%" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS3.p1.m4" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom /><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 8\%</annotation></semantics></math> --> ≈8%\approx 8\\% additional time overhead for a 27B model) even after the development of custom kernels and major infrastructure improvements to perform the Sinkhorn-Knopp iterations. KromHC and mHC-lite (in the small <!-- MathML: <math alttext="d" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS3.p1.m5" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> --> dd regime) both show significant speed ups due to the removal of the iterative updates. We here calculate the FLOP complexity of our method to show that it is superexponentially better than mHC-lite and incurs a small relative overhead compared to KromHC for the increased expressivity. For example, for <!-- MathML: <math alttext="d=16" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS3.p1.m6" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d=16</annotation></semantics></math> --> d=16d=16, the flop complexity of go-mHC is <!-- MathML: <math alttext="2" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS3.p1.m7" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math> --> 22 orders of magnitude slower than KromHC, compared to the <!-- MathML: <math alttext="16" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS3.p1.m8" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>16</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16</annotation></semantics></math> --> 1616 orders of magnitude imposed by mHC-lite. It is also approximately the same order of magnitude in complexity as mHC with SK iterations due to <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathcal{O}(d)\approx\mathcal{O}(S)" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS3.p1.m9" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(d)\approx\mathcal{O}(S)</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝒪⁡(d)≈𝒪⁡(S)\mathcal{O}(d)\approx\mathcal{O}(S).

In general, the model performance improvement is larger than the incurred computational
cost; however, when considering scaling the number of residual streams to allow for richer
topology, the complexity begins to set a practical limit – we hope to provide a
middle ground method that provides a good balance of incurred FLOP cost while maintaining
rich enough expressivity to allow for scaling.

units.text: The performance and convergence properties of <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathcal{P}_{\mathsf{M}}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S5.p1.m1" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mi>𝖬</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{P}_{\mathsf{M}}</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝒫𝖬\mathcal{P}_{\mathsf{M}} are fundamentally governed by the geometry of the underlying loss landscape introduced by <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathsf{M}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S5.p1.m2" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝖬</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathsf{M}</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝖬\mathsf{M} and the stability of the associated gradient signals. In the context of mHC this indicates that any target matrix should be reachable regardless of initial conditions using finite optimization iterations. We do expect go-mHC to have learnable gradients, be convergent and fully connected (able to get to any target matrix). See appendix [B.7](#A2.SS7 "B.7 Proofs of Coverage, Path Connectedness and Gradient Stability ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Derivations and Numerical Analysis ‣ go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-ConstrainedHyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices") for more details on this claim and associated proofs.
context: go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-Constrained  Hyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices

units.text: Not all matrix parameterizations are learnable and fully connected. mHC-lite should generally perform well by choosing a good initialization, but we suspect that this does not mitigate the fact that it may become very difficult to relearn an <!-- MathML: <math alttext="n" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S5.p2.m1" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> --> nn-stream transform after having previously converged as the model trains for longer due to the potential of vanishing gradients (a heuristic example is from needing to remap streams due to generalization). Numerics and further discussion can be found in the appendix [B.10](#A2.SS10 "B.10 Gradient Vanishing and Crosstalk in mHC-lite ‣ Appendix B Theoretical Derivations and Numerical Analysis ‣ go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-ConstrainedHyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices").
